translations.idiomatic: Late in Taixing robbers broke the tomb; he was moved to Dantu.

sentences.zh: 初，元帝鎮建鄴，裴妃之意也，帝深德之，數幸其第，以第三子沖奉越後。

translations.literal: At first, when Emperor Yuan garrisoned Jianye, it was Consort Pei's intent; the Emperor deeply valued her virtue, visited her mansion several times, and made his third son Chong heir to Yue's line.
translations.idiomatic: Consort Pei had urged Emperor Yuan to base himself at Jianye; grateful, he adopted her cause and let his third son Chong continue Yue's posterity.

sentences.zh: 薨，無子，成帝以少子奕繼之。

translations.literal: When she died she had no son; Emperor Cheng had his youngest son Yi continue the line.
translations.idiomatic: When Chong died without issue, Emperor Cheng placed his youngest son Yi in the line.

sentences.zh: 哀帝徙奕為琅邪王，而東海無嗣。

translations.literal: Emperor Ai moved Yi to Prince of Langye, and Donghai had no heir.
translations.idiomatic: Emperor Ai transferred Yi to Langye, leaving Donghai vacant.

sentences.zh: 隆安初，安帝更以會稽忠王次子彥璋為東海王，繼沖為曾孫。

translations.literal: At the start of Long'an, Emperor An again appointed Yanzhang, second son of Prince Zhong of Kuaiji, Prince of Donghai, to succeed Chong as great-grandson.
translations.idiomatic: Early in Long'an, Emperor An named Yanzhang, Prince Zhong of Kuaiji's second son, Prince of Donghai to continue Chong's line.

sentences.zh: 為桓玄所害，國除。

translations.literal: He was harmed by Huan Xuan, and the state was abolished.
translations.idiomatic: Huan Xuan killed him and abolished the fief.

sentences.zh: 史臣曰：昔高辛撫運，釁起參商；

translations.literal: The historians say: In antiquity the High Lord nurtured his fortune, yet strife arose between Shen and Shang;
translations.idiomatic: The chroniclers say: ancient Gaoxin saw strife flare between Shen and Shang.

sentences.zh: 宗周嗣曆，禍纏管、蔡。

translations.literal: The Zhou house inherited the calendar, but disaster tangled Guan and Cai.
translations.idiomatic: Zhou's succession snared Guan and Cai in revolt.

sentences.zh: 祥觀曩冊，逖聽前古，亂臣賊子，昭鑒在焉。

translations.literal: When one scans the registers of old and listens across former ages, rebellious ministers and traitorous sons stand reflected in the bright mirror.
translations.idiomatic: History leaves traitors nowhere to hide.

sentences.zh: 有晉鬱興，載崇籓翰，分茅錫瑞，道光恆典；

translations.literal: When Jin flourished, it honored its feudal bulwarks; it divided fiefs and granted auspicious tokens—its virtue shone in enduring canon;
translations.idiomatic: Jin ennobled kin, handed out jade tokens, and wrapped the act in shining precedent.

sentences.zh: 儀台飾袞，禮備彝章。

translations.literal: Its ceremonial terrace and ornamented robes completed the constant statutes of ritual.
translations.idiomatic: Regalia and ritual crowned each prince properly.

sentences.zh: 汝南以純和之姿，失於無斷；

translations.literal: The Prince of Runan, by a disposition purely mild, failed through indecision;
translations.idiomatic: Runan's gentle temper left him irresolute.

sentences.zh: 楚隱習果銳之性，遂成凶很。

translations.literal: The Hidden Prince of Chu, practicing sharp audacity, thereby became cruel and fierce.
translations.idiomatic: Chu's aggressive streak curdled into cruelty.

sentences.zh: 或位居朝右，或職參近禁，俱為女子所詐，相次受誅，雖曰自貽，良可哀也！

translations.literal: Some held rank at the court's right; some served within the forbidden precincts—all were deceived by women and executed one after another; though it is said they brought it on themselves, how pitiable!
translations.idiomatic: Whether at court or in the harem, women outplayed them—each died in turn, pitiable even if self-inflicted.

sentences.zh: 倫實庸瑣，見欺孫秀，潛構異圖，煽成奸慝。

translations.literal: Lun was truly mean and petty; deceived by Sun Xiu, he secretly framed a different plot and fanned treacherous evil.
translations.idiomatic: Lun was a vulgar pawn of Sun Xiu's conspiracy.

sentences.zh: 乃使元良遘怨酷，上宰陷誅夷，乾耀以之暫傾，皇綱於焉中圮。

translations.literal: Thereby he caused the crown prince to meet cruel resentment and the chief minister to fall to execution and slaughter—the heavenly radiance thereby tilted briefly, and the imperial net thereby broke mid-course.
translations.idiomatic: He destroyed the heir and top ministers; the throne flickered and the dynastic net tore.

sentences.zh: 遂裂冠毀冕，幸百六之會；

translations.literal: Then crowns were torn and caps destroyed, chancing upon the conjunction of the hundred and six;
translations.idiomatic: Regalia shattered when fate hit its crisis.

sentences.zh: 綰璽揚纛，窺九五之尊。

translations.literal: Seals were threaded and banners raised, spying on the honor of the Nine-and-Five.
translations.idiomatic: He grasped the seal and eyed the throne.

sentences.zh: 夫神器焉可偷安，鴻名豈容妄假！

translations.literal: How may the sacred vessel be seized in ease—how may the great name be falsely borrowed!
translations.idiomatic: The mandate cannot be stolen; the imperial style cannot be faked.

sentences.zh: 而欲托茲淫祀，享彼天年，凶暗之極，未之有也。

translations.literal: Yet wishing to rely on licentious sacrifice and enjoy those Heaven-allotted years—nothing could be darker or more vicious.
translations.idiomatic: Seeking long life through foul worship—nothing viler.

sentences.zh: 冏名父之子，唱義勤王，摧偽業于既成，拯皇輿於已墜，策勳考績，良足可稱。

translations.literal: Jiong was the son of a famed father; he raised righteousness and diligently served the king—he shattered the false enterprise once accomplished and raised the imperial carriage once fallen; his deeds merited praise in the assessment of merit.
translations.idiomatic: Jiong rallied loyal armies, broke the usurper, and restored the carriage—his record deserved praise.

sentences.zh: 然而臨禍忘憂，逞心縱欲，曾不知樂不可極，盈難久持，笑古人之未工，忘己事之已拙。

translations.literal: Yet facing calamity he forgot worry; he indulged his heart and gave rein to desire—never knowing that joy cannot reach its limit nor fullness endure long—he laughed that the ancients lacked skill and forgot how clumsy his own affairs had become.
translations.idiomatic: Yet amid peril he chased pleasure, mocked the wise, and missed his own folly.

sentences.zh: 向若采王豹之奇策，納孫惠之嘉謀，高謝袞章，永表東海，雖古之伊、霍，何以加焉！

translations.literal: Had he adopted Wang Bao's singular stratagem and accepted Sun Hui's fine counsel—high refusing the ceremonial robes and forever displaying integrity east of the sea—even the ancient Yi Yin and Huo Guang—what could add beyond that!
translations.idiomatic: Had he taken Wang Bao and Sun Hui's advice—abdicating glory for exile east of the sea—he might have rivaled Yi Yin or Huo Guang.

sentences.zh: 長沙材力絕人，忠概邁俗，投弓掖門，落落標壯夫之氣；

translations.literal: The Prince of Changsha's strength of materials surpassed others; his loyalty towered beyond custom—he cast aside his bow at Ye Gate and stood tall with the air of a stalwart;
translations.idiomatic: Changsha's Yi matched peerless courage with loyalty—at Ye Gate he dropped bow and stood like a champion.

sentences.zh: 馳車魏闕，懍懍懷烈士之風。

translations.literal: He raced his carriage at the Wei towers and clasped the wind of a martyr in awe.
translations.idiomatic: He drove on the Wei palace tiers with martyr fire in his eyes.

sentences.zh: 雖復陽九數屯，在三之情無奪。

translations.literal: Though the fate of "yang nine" repeated its oppression, the affection of "being in three" was not taken from him.
translations.idiomatic: Ill omens multiplied, yet kinship duty held.

sentences.zh: 撫其遺節，終始可觀。

translations.literal: Cherish his surviving integrity—beginning to end it invites regard.
translations.idiomatic: His steadfast honor stands clear from first to last.

sentences.zh: 穎既入總大權，出居重鎮，中台藉以成務，東夏資其宅心，乃協契河間，共圖進取。

translations.literal: Once Ying had entered to wield overall power and gone out to dwell on a heavy garrison, the central terrace relied on him to finish affairs and the eastern summer supplied his settled intent—then he joined covenant with Hejian to plot advance together.
translations.idiomatic: Ying ruled from court and camp alike, then allied with Prince Yong of Hejian for further grabs.

sentences.zh: 而顒任李含之狙詐，杖張方之陵虐，遂使武閔喪元，長沙授首，逞其無君之志，矜其不義之強。

translations.literal: Yet Yong employed Li Han's deceit and leaned on Zhang Fang's oppression—thereby Wu Min lost his head and Changsha yielded his neck; he displayed his lordless ambition and boasted of unrighteous strength.
translations.idiomatic: Yong wielded Li Han and Zhang Fang until Wu Min fell and Changsha died—flaunting treason and brute force.

sentences.zh: 鑾駕北巡，異乎有征無戰；

translations.literal: The imperial carriage toured north—unlike a campaign without battle;
translations.idiomatic: The imperial train went north—no peaceful punitive march.

sentences.zh: 乘輿西幸，非由望秩觀風。

translations.literal: The throne went west in favor—not by inspecting ranks and observing the winds.
translations.idiomatic: The throne fled west—not a ritual tour of the provinces.

sentences.zh: 若火燎原，猶可撲滅，矧茲安忍，能無及乎！

translations.literal: If fire spreads across the prairie it may still be extinguished—how much more such cruelty—how can calamity fail to arrive!
translations.idiomatic: Grassfires can be stamped out—this cruelty spread unchecked.

sentences.zh: 東海糾合同盟，創為義舉，匡復之功未立，陵暴之釁已彰，罄彼車徒，固求出鎮。

translations.literal: Donghai rallied allies in covenant and began a righteous undertaking; merit of restoration was not yet established, yet the offense of bullying supremacy was already manifest—he emptied those chariots and foot soldiers and insisted on seeking assignment beyond the capital.
translations.idiomatic: Donghai's league claimed restoration yet bullied the throne—before victory he drained the capital guard and bolted to a frontier command.

sentences.zh: 既而帝京寡弱，狡寇憑陵，遂令神器劫遷，宗社顛覆，數十萬眾並垂餌於豺狼，三十六王咸隕身於鋒刃。

translations.literal: Afterward the imperial capital was feeble; cunning bandits leaned upon it—thereupon the sacred vessel was seized and moved, the ancestral altars overturned; several hundred thousand hosts together hung as bait for wolves and jackals; thirty-six princes all fell upon blades.
translations.idiomatic: Luoyang collapsed; regalia moved, altars fell—hundreds of thousands fed wolves while thirty-six princes died by the sword.

sentences.zh: 禍難之極，振古未聞。

translations.literal: The extremity of calamity—unheard of since antiquity shook.
translations.idiomatic: No age had seen ruin so complete.

sentences.zh: 雖及焚如，猶為幸也。

translations.literal: Though it reached the burning annihilation (of Hexagram Li), still it counted as fortune.
translations.idiomatic: Even fiery slaughter seemed mercy beside what followed.

sentences.zh: 自惠皇失政，難起蕭牆，骨肉相殘，黎元塗炭，胡塵驚而天地閉，戎兵接而宮廟隳，支屬肇其禍端，戎羯乘其間隙，悲夫！

translations.literal: From Emperor Hui's loss of governance, hardship rose within the curtain wall—flesh and bone slew one another; the black-haired people were smeared in charcoal; Hu dust alarmed and Heaven and Earth closed; barbarian weapons met and palace temples ruined—the collateral branches began the disaster's edge; Rong and Jie rode the gap—alas!
translations.idiomatic: After Emperor Hui lost control, kin slaughtered kin while commoners burned; northern alarms sealed heaven and earth, barbarian blades smashed the palace—the princes opened the breach for Rong and Jie hordes—alas!

sentences.zh: 《詩》所謂「誰生厲階，至今為梗」，其八王之謂矣。

translations.literal: What the Book of Songs calls, "Who gave rise to the stairway of harm—it remains a stumbling block to this day"—that refers to these eight princes.
translations.idiomatic: As the Songs ask who carved the stairway of ruin still blocking the realm—these eight princes did.

sentences.zh: 贊曰：亮總朝政，瑋懷職競。

translations.literal: Encomium: Liang oversaw court government; Wei harbored rivalry for office.
translations.idiomatic: Encomium: Liang ran the court; Wei craved higher station.

sentences.zh: 讒巧乘間，豔妻過聽。

translations.literal: Slander and craft rode the gaps; a beautiful wife listened too credulously.
translations.idiomatic: Slander slipped through when favored wives believed too fast.

sentences.zh: 構怨連禍，遞遭非命。

translations.literal: They built up resentment and linked calamities; one after another they met violent deaths.
translations.idiomatic: Hatred chained into disaster; each prince died an unnatural death.

sentences.zh: 倫實下愚，敢竊龍圖，亂常奸位，遄及嚴誅。

translations.literal: Lun was truly base and foolish; he dared steal the dragon chart, violate constant norms, and usurp the throne—swiftly he met stern execution.
translations.idiomatic: Lun was a dull criminal who seized the dragon throne and paid at once with execution.

sentences.zh: 偉哉武閔！

translations.literal: How grand—Wu Min!
translations.idiomatic: The Grand Prince Wu Min!

sentences.zh: 首創宏謨。

translations.literal: He first devised the grand plan.
translations.idiomatic: He struck first for the righteous cause.

sentences.zh: 德之不建，良可悲夫！

translations.literal: Yet virtue was not established—how truly lamentable!
translations.idiomatic: Virtue never matched ambition—a bitter pity.

sentences.zh: 長沙奉國，始終靡慝；

translations.literal: Changsha served the state; from first to last he harbored no hidden evil.
translations.idiomatic: The Prince of Changsha served loyally without secret treachery.

sentences.zh: 功虧一簣，奄罹殘賊。

translations.literal: Merit lacked one basket-load—suddenly he fell to brutal bandits.
translations.idiomatic: Victory was one basket short—then rebels cut him down.

sentences.zh: 章度勤王，效立名揚；

translations.literal: Zhangdu (Ying) rallied to aid the king—deeds were achieved and fame raised.
translations.idiomatic: Zhangdu's Ying mobilized for the sovereign and won renown.

sentences.zh: 合從關右，犯順爭強，事窮勢蹙，俱為亂亡。

translations.literal: He allied west of the passes, defied obedience and strove for supremacy—affairs exhausted, straits pressed—both ended in rebellion and ruin.
translations.idiomatic: West-of-the-pass alliance turned into defiance—both camps collapsed together.

sentences.zh: 元超作輔，出征入撫，敗國喪師，無君震主。

translations.literal: Yuanchao served as regent—campaigning abroad and comforting within—ruining the state and losing armies—lordless toward his prince, alarming his sovereign.
translations.idiomatic: Yuanchao's Yue steered court and campaign yet ruined armies, snubbed his emperor, and terrified the throne.

sentences.zh: 焚如之變，抑惟自取。

translations.literal: The transformation of burning annihilation—perhaps nothing but what he invited himself.
translations.idiomatic: That fiery ending—nothing but self-invited ruin.
